bagegni.bio:
Dr. Nusayba Bagegni is a medical oncologist on the faculty of Washington University School of Medicine, where she holds the rank of Associate Professor of Medicine and sees breast cancer patients at Siteman Cancer Center. She is also associate medical director for clinical research in the oncology division, and she oversees its portfolio of breast cancer trials. She holds board certification in hematology, medical oncology and internal medicine.

Clinical trials are the core of her research, with emphasis on HER2-positive and metastatic disease, aggressive subtypes, breast cancer that arises in younger women, and early-phase drug development. She chairs a National Cancer Institute Experimental Therapeutics Clinical Trials Network study (NCT04345913) that pairs eribulin with copanlisib for metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. At Siteman she has led the local arm of several multicenter studies, including the ELAINE trials of lasofoxifene for ESR1-mutated disease, the two CompassHER2 trials and DESTINY-Breast06. In 2025 she was first author of a review in Cancers that answers practical questions about using trastuzumab deruxtecan when metastatic tumors are HER2-low or HER2-ultralow.

The National Cancer Institute chose Dr. Bagegni in 2024 for one of ten Early Career Cancer Clinical Investigator Awards given nationwide. She serves on the NCCN panel that writes the antiemesis guidelines. Teaching matters to her as well, and the WashU hematology/oncology fellows named her their Teacher of the Year in 2021.

Dr. Bagegni studied nutritional sciences at the University of Missouri and earned her MD at the University of Iowa's Carver College of Medicine in 2010. She then trained in internal medicine at WashU and Barnes-Jewish Hospital, spent two years as an instructor and bone marrow transplant hospitalist, and completed a hematology/oncology fellowship at WashU, where she served as co-chief fellow and was honored with the Hanna Jean Khoury award as an outstanding graduate. She joined the faculty as an assistant professor in 2018 and became an associate professor in 2024.

ballinger.bio:
Dr. Tarah Ballinger is a breast medical oncologist at Indiana University School of Medicine, where she is an associate professor and holds the Vera Bradley Foundation scholar title for breast cancer research. Her patients are seen at IU's Simon Comprehensive Cancer Center, where her clinical work covers treatment of breast cancer, follow-up care for survivors, and risk reduction for women at elevated risk through the Catherine Peachey Prevention Program. She created the center's Multidisciplinary Oncology Vitality and Exercise (MOVE) Program, which pairs people with any type of cancer with an individual exercise and physical therapy plan, and she is its medical director.

Dr. Ballinger's research looks at how the composition of the body, meaning bone, muscle and fat, together with physical activity, influences who develops cancer, how patients do, and which treatment side effects they experience. Breast cancer survivors are her main population, and she gives particular attention to muscle, a large tissue that has received little study in breast cancer even though many current drugs affect it. Her studies include exercise programs for people living with metastatic disease, a remote exercise program meant to lessen chemotherapy toxicity in Black women, and a test of low-intensity vibration for the joint and muscle problems that aromatase inhibitors can cause. She has also worked on disparities: in 2021 she led an IU analysis showing that excess weight was linked to more recurrences and deaths among women of African ancestry but not among women of European ancestry, and in 2026 she was lead author of a paper in Cancer on taxane-related nerve damage reported by Black patients. Earlier, using data from the BRE12-158 trial, she examined how body mass index relates to circulating tumor DNA and relapse following preoperative chemotherapy in triple-negative disease.

The Conquer Cancer Foundation of ASCO gave Dr. Ballinger a Career Development Award in 2019, and the Heroes Foundation's Catherine Peachey Fund has supported her research. She is a full member of the cancer center's Cancer Prevention and Control program and sits on the medical advisory board of Maple Tree Cancer Alliance, a nonprofit that delivers exercise programs to people with cancer. She also speaks to the public about staying active through every phase of cancer care.

Dr. Ballinger studied biochemistry and philosophy at Notre Dame, then earned her MD at Indiana University in 2012. After an internal medicine residency at Vanderbilt University, she returned to IU for her oncology fellowship, which she finished in 2017. She joined the IU faculty as an assistant professor, holding an oncology scholar title named for Sheila D. Ward, before her promotion to associate professor.

bardia.bio:
Dr. Aditya Bardia is a breast medical oncologist and Professor of Medicine in the hematology/oncology division at UCLA's David Geffen School of Medicine, which he joined in 2024. He directs the breast medical oncology program and oversees translational research integration for UCLA's Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center; he is also assistant chief for translational research in his division and leads the center's breast oncology disease site group. He sees patients at UCLA's Santa Monica Parkside cancer clinic.

Dr. Bardia's research connects laboratory findings with clinical trials of precision treatments for breast cancer, with antibody drug conjugates as a central theme. He guided sacituzumab govitecan through clinical testing, and it became the first antibody drug conjugate to win approval for triple-negative breast cancer that has spread; he was first author on both of its pivotal reports in the New England Journal of Medicine, including the phase 3 ASCENT trial. He likewise steered elacestrant through development, and it became the first oral selective estrogen receptor degrader approved for hormone receptor-positive metastatic disease; he was senior author of its phase 3 EMERALD trial. He was also first author of the phase 3 reports for trastuzumab deruxtecan in DESTINY-Breast06 (New England Journal of Medicine, 2024) and for datopotamab deruxtecan in TROPION-Breast01 (Journal of Clinical Oncology, 2025). A second line of his work uses circulating tumor cells and circulating tumor DNA as liquid biopsies to find new targets, choose therapy, track response and study resistance. His group has helped show how ESR1 mutations drive resistance to endocrine therapy, how RB1 alterations undermine CDK4/6 inhibitors, and how changes in both the antibody target and the payload target (TOP1) can make tumors resistant to an antibody drug conjugate.

Since December 2024 he has been editor in chief of the journal Breast Cancer Research and Treatment. Dr. Bardia is a Fellow of ASCO, and in 2026 the American Society for Clinical Investigation elected him a member. His other honors include a 2022 Distinguished Researcher Award from the Massachusetts Society of Clinical Oncologists (MSCO), an ASCO Young Investigator Award and two ASCO Merit Awards, the Dana-Farber/Harvard Cancer Center's Paul Calabresi K12 award, and three Douglas Family Foundation Prizes (2014, 2016 and 2020) at Massachusetts General Hospital. He was listed among highly cited researchers in 2023, 2024 and 2025, and he mentors fellows and junior faculty.

Dr. Bardia earned his MBBS at AIIMS in New Delhi and an MPH in epidemiology from the University of Iowa. He trained in internal medicine at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, where he received an institutional research award, and then did his medical oncology fellowship at the Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center, completing it in 2011. He spent more than a decade on the Harvard Medical School faculty at Massachusetts General Hospital, where he founded a molecular and precision medicine clinic for metastatic breast cancer and later directed breast cancer research at the Mass General Cancer Center before moving to UCLA.

birhiray.bio:
Dr. Ruemu Birhiray is a hematologist and medical oncologist in Indianapolis, where he is a partner at Hematology Oncology of Indiana, now part of American Oncology Network. He is an attending physician for medical oncology, hematology and stem cell transplantation at Ascension St. Vincent Hospital, and he teaches at Marian University's Wood College of Osteopathic Medicine, where he holds a clinical professorship. He holds board certification in medical oncology as well as internal medicine.

Dr. Birhiray started his practice's clinical research program and serves as a principal investigator on its studies. His projects have included a study, reported in 2006, of interferon alfa added to CHOP and rituximab for follicular lymphoma, and he has co-authored community-practice studies of proteasome inhibitor therapy for multiple myeloma. His earlier papers, in journals including the Journal of Clinical Oncology and Leukemia, dealt with antibody treatment of T-cell leukemia and with stem cell transplantation. He was senior author of a 2023 Blood Advances paper setting out DRIVE, a practical framework for making cancer clinical research more diverse, inclusive and accessible, and first author of a 2023 American Society of Hematology education article on conducting clinical research in community practice. In 2025 he joined expert roundtables for Blood Cancers Today on diffuse large B-cell and follicular lymphoma.

Medical education is a large part of his work. In 2002 Dr. Birhiray created the Indy Hematology Review, a yearly meeting for hematologists and oncologists that he continues to chair, and he leads its sponsoring nonprofit, Indy Hematology Education, as President and CEO. Indy Hematology Education also hosts meetings under the DRIVE name. He is a member of ASCO, the AMA and the American Society of Hematology.

Dr. Birhiray received his MD in Nigeria from the University of Benin. His internal medicine training took place at Chicago's Columbus Hospital, a Northwestern University affiliate, where he went on to serve as chief medical resident. He then completed a bone marrow transplant fellowship at Johns Hopkins and a medical oncology fellowship at the NCI in Bethesda, where his research explored gene therapy and cell-based immune treatments in the transplant setting. From 1998 to 2001 he directed the bone marrow transplant program at Marshfield Clinic in Wisconsin while holding a clinical faculty post at the University of Wisconsin, and in 2001 he received an associate professor appointment in transplantation at Rush University.

brufsky.bio:
Dr. Adam Brufsky is a breast medical oncologist on the faculty of the University of Pittsburgh, where he holds the rank of Professor of Medicine and serves as associate chief of hematology/oncology in the Department of Medicine. He is co-director of the university's Comprehensive Breast Cancer Center. At UPMC Hillman Cancer Center he co-directs the Cancer Therapeutics Program, and he is medical director of the women's cancer program based at UPMC Magee-Womens Hospital. His clinical work centers on breast cancer, especially metastatic disease. He holds board certification in medical oncology as well as internal medicine.

Dr. Brufsky's research spans new drug treatments for breast cancer, the interplay between bone and breast cancer, and the biology and management of metastatic disease. He led a pooled analysis of trials testing zoledronic acid to protect bone in women taking letrozole after surgery, and he has written on how bisphosphonates affect recurrence. He was first author of RIBBON-2, a phase 3 study that added bevacizumab to second-line chemotherapy for metastatic disease without HER2 overexpression, and of the registHER analysis of brain metastases in HER2-positive disease. He also contributed to TAILORx, the prospective test of the 21-gene recurrence assay, to the NSABP B-34 clodronate trial and to laboratory work on detecting ESR1 mutations in tumor tissue and blood. Heading the Pittsburgh Breast Cancer Consortium, funded by the Department of Defense, he has worked to bring metastatic breast cancer trials to community practices, and he has held grants from the NIH, Susan G. Komen and the Army's breast cancer research program.

Dr. Brufsky has held a series of leadership posts at the cancer center, serving as associate director for clinical investigation, for translational investigation and for strategic relationships. He has taught medical and nursing students and physicians in training, including as director of a course on neoplastic diseases. He also writes patient education on biomarker and circulating tumor cell testing for Living Beyond Breast Cancer. He is a Fellow of the American College of Physicians and a member of ASCO and the AACR.

Dr. Brufsky graduated cum laude in chemistry from Dartmouth College and completed a combined MD and PhD program at the University of Connecticut, with doctoral work in developmental biology. His internship and residency in internal medicine were at Brigham and Women's, and he then took fellowship training in medical oncology and marrow transplantation at Dana-Farber. Before coming to Pittsburgh he held appointments at Harvard as an instructor in medicine and associate physician.

cairo.bio:
Dr. Michelina Cairo is a medical oncologist with Texas Oncology in Houston, where she practices at the Memorial City office and focuses her care entirely on breast cancer. Her work includes treatment of the disease as well as breast cancer risk assessment and genetic evaluation, and she holds board certification in medical oncology.

Research has been part of Dr. Cairo's career since her training. Her practice takes part in studies aimed at finding better treatments, using the molecular subtype of each tumor to match patients with established and investigational drugs. She is a local principal investigator for Texas Oncology on FLEX, a large registry that links MammaPrint and BluePrint genomic profiles with patients' clinical data, and on ELEGANT, a phase 3 trial comparing elacestrant with standard endocrine therapy for early ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer at high risk of recurrence. In 2023 she spoke with OncLive about how side effects differ between two HER2-directed drugs used for metastatic disease, trastuzumab deruxtecan and trastuzumab emtansine.

During her fellowship Dr. Cairo chose a dedicated breast cancer research track, spending a full year in the Baylor College of Medicine laboratory of Jenny Chang and Mike Lewis. That work included co-authorship of a 2010 paper in Breast Cancer Research and Treatment on TGF-beta signaling and COX2 expression in breast tissue from high-risk women with dense mammograms. She also trained at MD Anderson Cancer Center in the care of breast cancer and sarcoma.

Dr. Cairo earned her bachelor's degree at Yale University, where she started a peer health education program for teenagers in New Haven middle schools. She also held a research fellowship in Senegal, studying whether health education for women led them to adopt new health practices. She completed medical school at Georgetown University in 2005 and then moved to Houston for internal medicine residency and a hematology/oncology fellowship, both at Baylor College of Medicine.

callahan.bio:
Dr. Rena Callahan is a hematologist and medical oncologist at UCLA Health who treats breast cancer exclusively, and she teaches as a member of the clinical faculty in medicine at UCLA's David Geffen School of Medicine. Her patients are seen at UCLA's cancer clinics in Santa Monica and in Valencia, in the Santa Clarita Valley. Her treatment planning draws on genomic testing, imaging and tumor biomarkers, and she makes a point of involving patients in each decision so that care reflects their own goals.

Dr. Callahan takes part in UCLA's breast cancer research program, and her current trials include the VIKTORIA-1 and VIKTORIA-2 studies of gedatolisib for advanced hormone receptor-positive disease. She was a coauthor of the TRIO-US B-09 trial, which tested everolimus with lapatinib and capecitabine in HER2-positive breast cancer that had spread to the brain, and of a 2018 Annals of Oncology report on ESR1 fusion proteins in tumors resistant to endocrine therapy. Her review writing covers HER2-positive disease, ado-trastuzumab emtansine and PARP inhibitors, and with Patricia Ganz she wrote the Diseases of the Breast textbook chapter on the neurocognitive, cardiac and second-cancer effects of systemic therapy. More recently she contributed to a 2025 ASCO Educational Book article on treatment after CDK4/6 inhibitors, co-writing its section on chemotherapy and antibody drug conjugates, and to a 2026 study comparing receptor status (ER, PR and HER2) in primary tumors with that of their lymph node metastases.

Dr. Callahan was listed among Castle Connolly Top Doctors each year from 2018 through 2025 and has been named a Southern California Super Doctor every year since 2021, after earlier recognition as a Rising Star. She speaks regularly at regional and national meetings on advances in breast cancer treatment.

Dr. Callahan studied biology at Yale University and earned her MD from the University of Pennsylvania in 2004, graduating with high honors and election to Alpha Omega Alpha. She completed all of her postgraduate training at UCLA, from internal medicine internship and residency through a fellowship in hematology and medical oncology that she completed in 2011.

conlin.bio:
Dr. Alison Conlin is a medical oncologist in Portland, Oregon, at the Providence Cancer Institute, where she heads the medical oncology side of the institute's breast cancer program. She cares for people with breast cancer at every stage, along with women who have high-risk breast conditions, and she sees patients at the Franz Clinic. She is board certified in medical oncology and internal medicine.

Much of Dr. Conlin's research is about giving patients access to clinical trials and to new drugs as they emerge. She has written trials for advanced breast cancer and for breast cancer that has spread to the brain, she was a coauthor of a phase 2 study of patupilone for breast cancer brain metastases, and she was a coauthor of the phase 1b tucatinib trials that paired the drug with ado-trastuzumab emtansine or with capecitabine and trastuzumab. Earlier work includes phase 2 studies of nab-paclitaxel combinations for metastatic disease. She is one of the principal investigators of the Pacific Cancer Research Consortium, a community site in the NCI Community Oncology Research Program, and she previously led the Western Oncology Research Consortium. Her recent collaborations include the 2026 NSABP B-35 analysis of lumpectomy margins in DCIS and a 2026 study of immune-priming cytokines given before neoadjuvant therapy for triple-negative breast cancer.

Dr. Conlin also has a background in health services and prevention research. With the American Cancer Society she studied cancer screening, prevention and care after testing as part of the Oregon Health Study, contributing to research on how gaining Medicaid coverage affects cancer screening. She has also written about cognitive symptoms reported by survivors after chemotherapy. She shares her clinical perspective through expert education programs, including a 2022 discussion of the ASCENT trial of sacituzumab govitecan and a 2026 case series about early-stage HER2-positive disease.

Dr. Conlin earned her MD at SUNY Upstate Medical University in 2002 and trained in internal medicine at NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital (Columbia and Cornell). She then moved to Memorial Sloan Kettering for her oncology fellowship, finishing in 2008. She also holds a master of public health from Boston University, where she concentrated on health services research.

dietrich.bio:
Dr. Martin Dietrich is a hematologist and medical oncologist in Rockledge, Florida, where his practice, Cancer Care Centers of Brevard, is part of The US Oncology Network. He also holds the rank of assistant professor of internal medicine in UCF's College of Medicine in Orlando. His clinical work covers the full range of blood disorders and cancers, with particular emphasis on lung and breast cancer and on genetic evaluation and counseling for inherited cancer syndromes and tumor mutations. He holds board certification in medical oncology as well as internal medicine, and he is a Fellow of the ACP.

Dr. Dietrich's research centers on precision oncology. He serves as a principal investigator on trials of new anticancer drugs, including studies run through the Sarah Cannon Research Institute, and he approaches treatment by matching therapy to the molecular features of each patient's tumor. His translational work examines genetic testing methods and blood-based liquid biopsies, and how biomarker results can be put to better use in everyday practice. He was first author of a 2016 JAMA Oncology diagnostic test interpretation article on using next-generation sequencing to find targetable alterations in tumors, and he co-authored a 2024 JCO Precision Oncology study showing that liquid biopsy done before a tissue diagnosis was linked to faster start of lung cancer treatment.

Dr. Dietrich speaks often, in the United States and abroad, on molecular genetics, immunotherapy and thoracic cancers. His recent education programs include 2026 series with Ticiana Leal on lung cancers that carry HER2 mutations and on ROS1-positive lung cancer, a program on immunotherapy around surgery for resectable lung cancer, and a 2022 series on preventing chemotherapy-induced bone marrow suppression in extensive-stage small cell lung cancer. He belongs to ASCO, AACR, ASH, ESMO, IASLC and FLASCO, the Florida oncology society.

Dr. Dietrich received his medical degree from Ruprecht Karl University in Heidelberg and earned two doctorates: one in cancer biology, completed in Heidelberg at the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), plus one in molecular genetics from UT Southwestern in Dallas. He remained at UT Southwestern for residency and for hematology/oncology fellowship in its physician-scientist track, with support from an NCI T32 training grant. Before joining Cancer Care Centers of Brevard he practiced with Florida Cancer Specialists & Research Institute, which he joined in 2020.

gadi.bio:
Dr. VK Gadi is a medical oncologist and physician-scientist in Chicago, where he is Deputy Director of the UI Cancer Center (University of Illinois). At UIC's College of Medicine he holds the rank of Professor of Medicine and leads medical oncology within the hematology and oncology division as its director. His clinical practice at UI Health is devoted to breast cancer at every stage, delivered through a team approach that aims to match each patient with the most effective treatment and the fewest side effects. He is board certified in internal medicine and medical oncology.

Dr. Gadi's research runs from the laboratory to the clinic. His lab has studied cancer biology, tumor immunology and diagnostics, with interests in breast cancer, immunotherapy and the use of functional genetics to find new drug targets. He directs the cancer center's phase 1 program, where first-in-human studies of new agents for advanced solid tumors work out doses, schedules and the patients most likely to benefit. He is an inventor on patents covering cancer therapy, diagnostic tests and transplantation, and he works with UIC's technology transfer office to license discoveries. In 2026 he and Bin He received a cancer center pilot award to develop a targeted oncolytic herpes simplex virus immunotherapy, and he was one of the investigators given the center's Team Science Award for a proposal to build blood vessel routes that carry immune cells into metastatic breast tumors.

Since arriving in Chicago in 2020, Dr. Gadi has focused on building the solid tumor clinical and research workforce serving Cook County, the area the cancer center is charged with covering. He brings promising investigational drugs from large and small companies into the center's trial portfolio, has expanded its role in national cooperative group studies, and helps disease teams design trials that fit the patients they serve. He has spoken about mentorship and equitable care on medical podcasts and, in 2026, joined a panel on widening access to HER2-targeted therapies.

Dr. Gadi earned both his MD and PhD at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. He then moved to Seattle, completing an internal medicine residency with the University of Washington before an oncology fellowship at Fred Hutchinson. He spent about two decades there, rising to associate professor on the UW faculty, before moving to UIC.

garrido-castro.bio:
Dr. Ana Garrido-Castro is a breast medical oncologist in Boston at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, where she directs research on triple-negative breast cancer for the breast oncology division of the Susan F. Smith Center for Women's Cancers. She holds a faculty appointment at Harvard Medical School as Assistant Professor of Medicine. Her clinical interests include triple-negative disease, immunotherapy, targeted treatments, new drug development and the search for predictive biomarkers.

Dr. Garrido-Castro's research aims to find better treatments for breast cancer, with triple-negative breast cancer as her main focus. She leads clinical trials of immune checkpoint therapy, targeted agents and antibody drug conjugates, and in 2026 she was first author of two randomized phase 2 reports: one asking whether adding nivolumab to carboplatin helps patients with metastatic triple-negative disease (Nature Communications), and SACI-IO HR+, which asked the same question of pembrolizumab added to sacituzumab govitecan in metastatic hormone receptor-positive disease (Annals of Oncology). Earlier in her career, with a grant from the Terri Brodeur Breast Cancer Foundation, she studied tumors that begin as hormone receptor-positive but become triple-negative when they spread, comparing their genomic and immune features with those of tumors that are triple-negative from the start. Funding for her work has come from the National Cancer Institute, Komen, BCRF, the Conquer Cancer Foundation, METAvivor, the Breast Cancer Alliance, the Terri Brodeur Breast Cancer Foundation and the Triple Negative Breast Cancer Foundation.

In 2023 Dr. Garrido-Castro received a joint Conquer Cancer and Triple Negative Breast Cancer Foundation award supporting advanced clinical research in this disease. Her earlier honors include BCRF's Marion R. Wright award, which recognizes scientific excellence, a Komen Career Catalyst grant, the Conquer Cancer Foundation's Gianni Bonadonna Breast Cancer Research Fellowship (2017) and a METAvivor Early Career Investigator Award (2018). She teaches widely on treatment of triple-negative disease, including how to choose and sequence antibody drug conjugates and how to care for patients who relapse soon after chemoimmunotherapy, and she has spoken at the NCI's meeting on early drug development.

Dr. Garrido-Castro earned her medical degree at the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid and trained in medical oncology at Vall d'Hebron University Hospital in Barcelona. She came to Dana-Farber in 2016 for its advanced fellowship in breast oncology, which she combined with a Harvard research fellowship, and then joined the faculty.

gradishar.bio:
Dr. William Gradishar is a breast medical oncologist in Chicago at Northwestern University's Feinberg School of Medicine, where he holds the Betsy Bramsen professorship in breast oncology and is Professor of Medicine in hematology and oncology. He has been chief of Feinberg's hematology and oncology division since 2018. He also directs the Maggie Daley Center for Women's Cancer Care at Northwestern's Lurie cancer center, leading the development and conduct of clinical trials of new breast cancer treatments.

Dr. Gradishar's research focuses on bringing new therapies to patients with breast cancer, in both the adjuvant and metastatic settings. His work spans endocrine therapy, chemotherapy and targeted agents, and he often teaches clinicians how to fit new drugs, such as HER2-directed antibody drug conjugates, into everyday treatment decisions. He has also taken part in expert discussions on preventing chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.

Dr. Gradishar chairs the NCCN panel that writes the breast cancer treatment guidelines and also serves on its breast cancer risk reduction panel. He founded the Lynn Sage Breast Cancer Symposium at Lurie in 1998 and has chaired it ever since. He is a deputy editor of NEJM Clinician (formerly NEJM Journal Watch) and a past editor in chief of Breast Cancer Research and Treatment, and his editorial board service includes Clinical Breast Cancer, Oncology, the Journal of Clinical Oncology and Current Treatment Options in Oncology. Other national roles include consulting for the FDA's Oncologic Drugs Advisory Committee (ODAC), service on the ECOG (now ECOG-ACRIN) breast cancer committee and study section work for the NIH, the Department of Defense, the American Cancer Society and Komen, and he has chaired several ASCO committees, among them the Oncology Training Program Committee. In 2016 he chaired the breast cancer working group of Cancer MoonShot 2020, a research coalition led by Patrick Soon-Shiong. ASCO has named him a Fellow (FASCO), as has the American College of Physicians (FACP).

Dr. Gradishar received his medical degree from the University of Illinois at Chicago College of Medicine. He completed residency at Michael Reese Hospital and Medical Center and a fellowship at the University of Chicago.

hamilton.bio:
Dr. Erika Hamilton is a medical oncologist in Nashville and a research leader at Sarah Cannon Research Institute (SCRI). Since January 2026 (the appointment was announced in October 2025) she has been SCRI's Chief Development Officer for late-phase research, heading its late-stage oncology studies, working with industry partners on the institute's Accelero strategy, and leading teams that design new kinds of trials and build personalized medicine into them. She has directed SCRI's breast cancer research since 2015, setting the direction of that program at sites throughout the SCRI network. She treats patients with breast and gynecologic cancers through SCRI Oncology Partners and holds board certification in medical oncology.

Dr. Hamilton came to SCRI in 2013 to work on drug development for cancers affecting women, and early-phase studies of new agents remain central to her work. For several years she led research in both breast and gynecologic cancers. Her recent publications include the phase 2 ELAINE 1 trial comparing lasofoxifene with fulvestrant in ESR1-mutated metastatic breast cancer, a basket study of tucatinib with trastuzumab in HER2-positive biliary tract cancer, and a trial of selinexor as maintenance therapy for endometrial cancer. At the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting she gave an oral presentation on subgroup results for tucatinib added to maintenance trastuzumab and pertuzumab in metastatic HER2-positive disease. She encourages patients to ask about trials at diagnosis rather than as a last resort, and supports SCRI's aim of offering them close to home. She also takes part in patient education programs on new breast cancer treatments.

Dr. Hamilton was the scientific program chair of ASCO's 2025 annual meeting. Her other ASCO service includes chairing its scientific committee on metastatic breast cancer (2019 to 2020), sitting on the 2023 plenary committee and, since 2024, the Cancer Research Committee, completing the Leadership Development Program, and a 2025 to 2028 term on the Nominating Committee. From 2023 to 2025 she co-chaired the scientific committee for ESMO's annual breast cancer meeting. She is an associate editor of Clinical Breast Cancer and reviews manuscripts for journals such as JCO and NEJM. In 2021 she co-chaired the first Great Debates and Updates in Women's Oncology conference, leading its breast cancer program. She is a Fellow of ASCO (FASCO). In 2021 Nashville Medical News included her among its Women to Watch.

Dr. Hamilton graduated from Washington and Lee University and was awarded an NCAA Postgraduate Scholarship. Afterward she returned to North Carolina, earning her MD and completing internal medicine residency at UNC Chapel Hill, and went on to Duke University for her hematology/oncology fellowship, where she was a finalist for a teaching award given by house staff.

iyengar.bio:
Dr. Neil Iyengar is a breast medical oncologist in Atlanta at Emory's Winship Cancer Institute. On the Emory School of Medicine faculty he is an Associate Professor in hematology and medical oncology, and he co-directs the breast medical oncology program. As Winship's Director of Survivorship Services, he shapes how survivorship care is organized across Winship and Emory Healthcare, including individualized wellness plans that address exercise, nutrition and supportive care, and he guides research in this area. He sees patients on Winship's Clifton Road campus, is a clinical member of the Glenn Family Breast Center, and is board certified in medical oncology and internal medicine.

Dr. Iyengar's research asks how metabolic health shapes cancer risk and treatment. His team described inflammation of the fatty tissue of the breast, a process that increases estrogen signaling and was found in most patients with obesity and in some without it. In a 2019 JAMA Oncology analysis of about 3,500 postmenopausal women of normal weight from the Women's Health Initiative, he and his colleagues found that those with the most body fat were close to twice as likely to develop invasive breast cancer. He has tested structured exercise and diet programs for people at high risk of or living with breast cancer, and he studies whether drugs used for diabetes and obesity can make cancer therapy work better. At Memorial Sloan Kettering he led a series of trials on breast cancer, fat tissue inflammation and therapeutic exercise, including an NCI-supported study designed to find the right amount of physical activity for patients whose cancer has spread. Funding for this work has come from the National Cancer Institute, Conquer Cancer, the American Cancer Society and BCRF.

Dr. Iyengar serves as one of the two editors in chief of ONCOLOGY, is an associate editor for npj Breast Cancer, and sits on the editorial board of the AACR journal Cancer Prevention Research. His honors include a Conquer Cancer career development award, an American Cancer Society Research Scholar Award (2019), a 2023 Oncology Hero Award given by Physician Education Resources, and a young investigator award from Expedition Inspiration. He also hosts clinician education programs on biomarker testing and on treating breast cancers that are hormone receptor-positive.

Dr. Iyengar earned both his undergraduate and medical degrees in Chicago, completing an accelerated University of Illinois program, finishing with the university's top honors. His residency in internal medicine was at the University of Chicago, and he then completed an oncology and hematology fellowship at Memorial Sloan Kettering. He spent the next years on the MSK breast medicine service as an associate attending physician, founding the MSK Healthy Living Program and leading the Breast Medicine Service's Optimal Living Program, while also holding faculty and research appointments at Weill Cornell Medicine and Rockefeller University. He moved to Emory in 2025.

jhaveri.bio:
Dr. Komal Jhaveri is a breast medical oncologist in New York, practicing at MSK (Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center), who specializes in early-phase drug development. Within MSK's Breast Medicine Service she heads the Endocrine Therapy Research Program as section head; she is also clinical director of the MSK Early Drug Development Service, where she sees patients as an associate attending physician. She holds an associate professorship in medicine at Weill Cornell Medicine.

Dr. Jhaveri's research seeks better treatments for breast cancer through clinical trials that are built together with biomarker studies of tumor tissue, circulating tumor DNA and imaging. She has led the clinical development of many targeted agents, among them inhibitors of PI3K and AKT, FGFR, HER2 and KAT6, selective cell-cycle inhibitors, new endocrine drugs and antibody drug conjugates. Her work includes the first human trial of the oral SERD AZD9496, the multi-tumor study of HER kinase inhibition in HER2- and HER3-mutant cancers published in Nature, and the INAVO120 trial of inavolisib. She also helped test HER2-targeted PET imaging with zirconium-89 pertuzumab, and her recent work focuses on companion imaging and radioligand approaches that pair detection of a biomarker with a treatment aimed at it. BCRF has supported her work as one of its investigators since 2025.

Dr. Jhaveri co-chairs the endocrine resistance working group of TBCRC, a national consortium for translational breast cancer research, and serves on the molecular tumor board of ASCO's TAPUR study. At MSK she holds the Patricia and James Cayne Chair for Junior Faculty. She has received a Conquer Cancer Young Investigator Award and is a Fellow of both ASCO and the American College of Physicians. She presents regularly at ASCO, AACR, ESMO and SABCS, and her work has appeared in journals including Annals of Oncology, JCO and NEJM.

Dr. Jhaveri received her MD from the University of Mumbai and also trained in nuclear medicine in Mumbai. She completed internal medicine residency at St. Luke's-Roosevelt Hospital Center in New York (now part of Mount Sinai) and then entered MSK's medical oncology and hematology fellowship. From 2012 to 2015 she was an assistant professor of medicine at NYU, practicing at NYU Langone and Bellevue Hospital, before rejoining MSK.

kang.bio:
Dr. Irene Kang is a breast medical oncologist in Irvine, California, at City of Hope's Lennar Foundation Cancer Center, where she leads women's health medical oncology as its medical director. She holds the rank of Assistant Professor in City of Hope's medical oncology and therapeutics research department. Her clinical work is devoted to the diagnosis and treatment of breast cancer, and she is board certified in medical oncology, hematology and internal medicine.

Dr. Kang's research spans early-phase clinical trials, the molecular makeup of individual breast tumors, and the management of symptoms and survivorship. At City of Hope's Orange County campus she is principal investigator of ENDORSE, a study registered in 2026 that tests whether a report of biology-based treatment recommendations helps doctors choose therapy for advanced hormone receptor-positive disease. Within the SWOG RxPONDER trial, she led an analysis of patient-reported cognitive function, published in JAMA Oncology in 2026, which found that women who received chemotherapy before endocrine therapy reported more problems with memory and concentration than those treated with endocrine therapy alone, in some cases lasting three years; she has pointed to these results as a reason to use genomic risk tests to spare chemotherapy when it offers little benefit. Earlier work with colleagues at USC examined circulating tumor cells, interval exercise training during chemotherapy and disparities in emergency care after breast surgery.

Dr. Kang takes part in national research and quality efforts through ASCO and SWOG. At USC she was the physician lead for ASCO's Quality Oncology Practice Initiative and served on committees overseeing fellowship education and clinical research. USC's oncology fellows honored her with a teaching award in 2020, and Los Angeles magazine has listed her among the region's top doctors.

Dr. Kang studied bioengineering at the University of California, Berkeley, where she was elected to Phi Beta Kappa, and received her medical degree from UCSF. She trained as an internal medicine resident in San Jose (Santa Clara Valley Medical Center), then completed a hematology/oncology fellowship at USC and LAC+USC Medical Center, serving as co-chief fellow. She was on the USC faculty from 2017 until joining City of Hope in 2022.

krie.bio:
Dr. Amy Krie is a breast cancer specialist in medical oncology at Allina Health Cancer Institute in Minneapolis, based at Abbott Northwestern Hospital. She sees patients at the institute's Piper Breast Center in Plymouth. Her board certification is in medical oncology. She treats breast cancer as a team effort, coordinating closely with the surgeons, plastic surgeons, radiologists, pathologists and radiation oncologists involved in each patient's care, and she places a strong emphasis on helping patients understand their options as treatment choices grow more complex. In 2024 she spoke on Minnesota Public Radio about the rise in breast cancer among women younger than 50 and about treatment advances that are improving survival.

Dr. Krie takes part in clinical research alongside her practice. At Abbott Northwestern she is the local principal investigator for PIKALO-2, a phase 2/3 study of the PI3K-alpha inhibitor tersolisib for people whose advanced breast cancer carries a PIK3CA alteration. She is a coauthor of the COMET trial, which compared active monitoring with standard treatment in women with low-risk DCIS, and of its analysis of patient-reported outcomes, both published in 2025, and of a 2026 analysis from the EA1181 trial examining complete pathologic response rates when taxane, trastuzumab and pertuzumab are given before surgery for HER2-positive disease. Earlier she was a coauthor of the I-PREDICT studies, which used molecular profiling of each patient's cancer to choose individualized drug combinations, with results published in Nature Medicine in 2019 and Genome Medicine in 2021.

Dr. Krie earned her MD in 2001 from the University of Iowa's Carver College of Medicine and completed internal medicine residency at Oregon Health & Science University, where mentors on the oncology service drew her to the field. She returned to the University of Iowa for her hematology/oncology fellowship, finishing in 2006. She then practiced in Sioux Falls, where in 2018 she was one of the breast cancer medical oncologists at Avera Cancer Institute, before joining Allina Health.

krop.bio:
Dr. Ian Krop is a breast medical oncologist in New Haven, where he holds the rank of Professor of Internal Medicine on the Yale School of Medicine faculty. In June 2026 he was named chief of Yale's Section of Medical Oncology and Hematology; at the same time he became Smilow Cancer Hospital and Yale Cancer Center's Deputy Director for Clinical Affairs. His clinical practice at Smilow is focused on breast cancer.

Dr. Krop's translational research centers on new targeted drugs and immune-based treatments for breast cancer and on understanding why tumors become resistant to them, with most of his effort devoted to HER2-positive disease. He played a leading role in the clinical development of two HER2-directed antibody drug conjugates, T-DM1 (trastuzumab emtansine) and trastuzumab deruxtecan. His studies have also examined treatment given before surgery, genomic tools such as an 80-gene signature for predicting who benefits from adding pertuzumab (from the APHINITY trial), and the meaning of PIK3CA mutations in HER2-positive disease. He was a coauthor of a 2026 Lancet Oncology analysis from the APHINITY trial comparing manual, digital and artificial intelligence scoring of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. BCRF has funded his research since 2017.

Nationally, Dr. Krop is chief scientific officer of TBCRC, a consortium of academic centers running translational breast cancer trials, and he helps lead correlative science for the Alliance cooperative group as one of its co-vice chairs. He is on the National Cancer Institute's steering committee for breast cancer, sits on ECOG-ACRIN's data monitoring committee, and has served on safety monitoring boards for several phase 3 trials.

Dr. Krop completed his undergraduate studies, MD and a PhD in biochemistry, cellular and molecular biology at Johns Hopkins, followed by internal medicine residency at the Johns Hopkins Hospital. He then trained as a hematology/oncology fellow at Dana-Farber, and he remained on its faculty, rising to associate chief of breast oncology there and to associate professor at Harvard Medical School. He joined Yale in 2022 to lead the cancer center's clinical research as chief clinical research officer, also serving as medical director of its Clinical Trials Office; his 2026 appointments give him broad oversight of clinical trials and clinical research across Yale Cancer Center and Smilow.

kruse.bio:
Dr. Megan Kruse is a medical oncologist in Cleveland who specializes in breast cancer. In January 2026 Cleveland Clinic named her Director of Breast Medical Oncology; she also co-leads its Breast Cancer Program. She has also run the Taussig Cancer Center's Clinical Trials Office as its medical director since July 2025, after directing the clinic's breast cancer clinical research starting in 2024.

Dr. Kruse's research is aimed at improving care for people with invasive lobular breast cancer, and she has a particular interest in the immune environment of these tumors and whether it could open the door to immunotherapy. She created Cleveland Clinic's Comprehensive Lobular Breast Cancer Program, which combines a dedicated clinical pathway for lobular disease, a coordinated research effort and a philanthropic fund for related projects. Her earlier studies examined how inherited variation in the HSD3B1 gene might influence estrogen-driven breast cancer and response to endocrine therapy with CDK4/6 inhibitors, compared outcomes of pleomorphic and classic lobular carcinoma, and, during fellowship, produced a phase 2 trial design for a folate receptor alpha-targeted antibody drug conjugate in metastatic triple-negative disease.

Dr. Kruse is active in national cooperative group research. For NRG Oncology she serves on the breast cancer core, translational research and developmental therapeutics committees, and she has represented NRG on the NCI task force for breast immuno-oncology. She is also a member of the NSABP Foundation's core research committee, an associate editor of ASCO Daily News and a scientific advisor to the Lobular Breast Cancer Alliance. She regularly teaches clinicians and patients about HER2-positive breast cancer and about treatment options for ESR1-mutated disease.

Dr. Kruse earned her medical degree at Case Western Reserve University and trained in internal medicine at UPMC in Pittsburgh. She returned to Cleveland for fellowship training in hematology/oncology at Cleveland Clinic, served as chief fellow, and joined the staff in 2017. From 2020 to 2024 she was associate program director of the Cleveland Clinic hematology/oncology fellowship.

lustberg.bio:
Dr. Maryam Lustberg is a breast medical oncologist in New Haven who leads breast cancer care at Yale in two roles: she heads the Center for Breast Cancer run jointly by Yale Cancer Center and Smilow Cancer Hospital, and she is Yale Cancer Center's Chief of Breast Medical Oncology. On the Yale School of Medicine faculty she is a Professor of Internal Medicine in medical oncology. She cares for patients with every stage and type of breast cancer and places a strong emphasis on shared decision-making.

Dr. Lustberg's research focuses on the side effects of breast cancer treatment and on how to improve the long-term health of survivors. She is also developing blood-based biomarkers that could signal recurrence or treatment toxicity earlier. Her studies have addressed nerve damage from chemotherapy, early detection of heart injury using cardiac MRI and blood markers, changes in thinking and memory during chemotherapy, and the loss of balance and higher fall risk that some patients experience after treatment. She has tested food-based and anti-inflammatory approaches, including omega-3 fatty acids and curcumin for joint pain caused by aromatase inhibitors, and more recently a pilot trial of minocycline to protect mood and cognition during chemotherapy. An NCI-funded investigator, she is active in the Alliance and SWOG cooperative groups.

Dr. Lustberg became president of MASCC, the international society devoted to supportive care in cancer, in June 2022, and she is an associate editor of the Journal of Cancer Survivorship. Within ASCO she has served on the Annual Meeting Education Committee, the neuropathy guideline panel and the education committee on patient and survivor care, and she took part in its Leadership Development Program. ASCO named her a Fellow (FASCO) in 2024. Her other honors include an ASCO Young Investigator Award, recognition from Forbes among the country's top breast medical oncologists, Castle Connolly's Exceptional Women in Medicine award in 2020, and teaching and mentoring awards from fellows and medical students. She works with patient advocacy groups to improve shared decision-making and trial participation, and she has spoken at Living Beyond Breast Cancer's conference on metastatic disease.

Dr. Lustberg studied biochemistry and English as an undergraduate at the University of Maryland and stayed there for medical school and internal medicine residency. She then completed fellowships in both medical oncology and breast oncology at Ohio State, where she also earned an MPH in clinical investigation, and joined its faculty in 2010. At Ohio State she directed the James cancer center's program for breast cancer survivors and led supportive care before moving to Yale in 2021.

makhlin.bio:
Dr. Igor Makhlin is an oncologist specializing in breast cancer at Penn Medicine's Abramson Cancer Center, where he holds the rank of assistant professor of clinical medicine within Penn's Division of Hematology-Oncology. His clinical practice is weighted toward HER2-positive disease. At Penn he is the site principal investigator for ATEMPT 2.0, a phase 2 trial comparing adjuvant trastuzumab emtansine with paclitaxel and trastuzumab in early HER2-positive disease, and for ETHAN, a phase 2 study of endocrine therapy for breast cancer in men.

His research touches treatment selection, tumor biology and the heart. Dr. Makhlin was first author of the 2024 ASCO Guideline Clinical Insights article in JCO Oncology Practice on how to select and order targeted therapies in metastatic HR-positive breast cancer, and he wrote a 2024 JAMA Network Open commentary on using genomic assays to judge whether extended endocrine therapy is worthwhile, followed in 2026 by a commentary on molecular profiling and guideline-concordant care. He was first author of a phase 2 trial of ruxolitinib with exemestane for advanced ER-positive disease that had stopped responding to aromatase inhibitors. In cardio-oncology, he led an analysis from the randomized PREVENT trial showing that statins did not meaningfully change markers of oxidative and nitrosative stress, and he contributed to a study of cardiovascular complications linked to CDK4/6 inhibitors. He is also a coauthor of the randomized phase 2 CLEVER trial, published in Nature Medicine in 2025, which tested hydroxychloroquine, everolimus or both against dormant tumor cells as a way to prevent recurrence.

Dr. Makhlin directs Penn's tumor board for metastatic breast cancer and serves as Penn's clinical leader for the breast pathways within Flatiron Assist. He teaches in Penn's continuing medical education programs on breast cancer, gave a keynote on managing treatment side effects at Living Beyond Breast Cancer's 2025 metastatic conference, spoke at its 2026 summit, and has given educational talks on ESR1-mutant metastatic disease and on FES-PET/CT imaging.

Dr. Makhlin completed his undergraduate degree at Penn State in 2009 and earned his MD in 2015 at The Commonwealth Medical College (now Geisinger Commonwealth School of Medicine). His residency in internal medicine was at Johns Hopkins Hospital. He then returned to Pennsylvania for fellowship training in hematology and medical oncology at Penn. Earlier, from 2009 to 2011, he did laboratory work on mTOR signaling in urothelial carcinoma.

mardones.bio:
Dr. Mabel Mardones is a Denver-based partner at Rocky Mountain Cancer Centers, part of The US Oncology Network, where her practice is devoted to breast cancer. She is board certified in hematology, medical oncology and internal medicine. She cares for patients with every type of breast cancer, with particular attention to young women, as well as for women at elevated risk of developing the disease. She uses genomic testing to tailor treatment, reviews cases at a weekly breast tumor board, and sees patients in both English and Spanish at the practice's Denver location on the Rose Medical Center campus and at its Lone Tree office at Sky Ridge.

Clinical research is a steady part of her community practice. Dr. Mardones sits on SCRI's breast cancer research executive committee; SCRI (Sarah Cannon Research Institute) is the research network her practice belongs to. She is a coauthor of the primary analysis of the phase 3 persevERA trial, a late-breaking abstract at the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting that compared first-line giredestrant plus palbociclib with letrozole plus palbociclib for advanced disease that is ER-positive and HER2-negative. She has also commented on how TROP2-directed antibody-drug conjugates could reshape first-line treatment of metastatic triple-negative breast cancer.

Within the network, Dr. Mardones co-chairs the task force that sets breast cancer treatment pathways. She teaches in continuing medical education programs on endocrine-resistant ER-positive metastatic disease and on bringing next-generation SERDs into community care, and she moderated a 2024 regional session on HR-positive, HER2-negative treatment for the Institute for Value-Based Medicine.

Health equity is a recurring theme in her work. Dr. Mardones argues that trials should reach patients where they live and that eligibility criteria should better reflect the people being treated, and she spoke on a 2021 Colorado panel about Latinx cancer care and disparities in breast cancer outcomes.

Dr. Mardones completed her undergraduate studies at Southwestern Adventist University and her medical degree at Loma Linda University. After internship and internal medicine residency at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, she trained in hematology and oncology at Baylor University Medical Center in Dallas.

mcarthur.bio:
Dr. Heather McArthur is a medical oncologist and Clinical Director of UT Southwestern's breast cancer program, based at the Simmons Comprehensive Cancer Center, with responsibility for breast cancer care across the UTSW health system. She is a professor in UTSW's Department of Internal Medicine (hematology and oncology division), and has held UTSW's Komen Distinguished Chair in Clinical Breast Cancer Research since her arrival. She limits her own clinical practice to patients with breast cancer.

Dr. McArthur's research aims to improve how breast cancer is diagnosed and treated, and immunotherapy is its core. One line of her work pairs local tumor destruction, by cryoablation or by radiation, with immune-stimulating drugs in early-stage disease, on the idea that the combination may train the immune system to recognize the tumor over the long term. With Breast Cancer Research Foundation funding since 2013, her team is now running a phase 2 study that adds cryoablation to ipilimumab and nivolumab for triple-negative cancer left behind after standard preoperative treatment. She also co-led a trial, reported in 2025, that gave two doses of pembrolizumab with radiation before chemotherapy and surgery; in triple-negative disease it produced a pathologic complete response rate close to that of the standard regimen, with roughly half as much serious toxicity and a far shorter course of treatment. She is global principal investigator or co-principal investigator for four randomized phase 3 trials that test immunotherapy given with curative intent (TROPION-Breast04, TroFuse-012, IMpassion030 and CheckMate 7FL), and she sits on steering committees for other phase 3 studies. She was a coauthor of the 2020 NEJM report of the KEYNOTE-522 trial, which tested pembrolizumab in early-stage triple-negative disease, and of the Society for Immunotherapy of Cancer practice guideline on immunotherapy in breast cancer.

She has held many national and international roles. Dr. McArthur has co-chaired an immunotherapy taskforce of the Breast International Group and has served on the National Cancer Institute's breast immuno-oncology task force and on immuno-oncology groups within the Alliance cooperative group. For ASCO she has chaired the Annual Meeting's immuno-oncology scientific program committee, co-chaired its Practice Health Task Force, and served on education, clinical practice, grant selection and guideline panels. She is an associate editor of Breast Cancer Research and serves on the editorial boards of Cancer and of Breast Cancer Research and Treatment, and she is a Fellow of ASCO. Her honors include a 2019 Laura Ziskin Prize in Translational Research from Stand Up To Cancer.

A native of Canada, Dr. McArthur completed undergraduate studies at UBC in Vancouver before earning her MD from the University of Toronto. Her residency in internal medicine was in Calgary, followed by medical oncology fellowship at BC Cancer in Vancouver. A Canadian national fellowship award then brought her to Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center for advanced clinical research training focused on breast cancer. She also earned an MPH from Harvard, concentrating on clinical trial design. As MSK faculty she built the center's breast cancer immunotherapy program, and from 2016 she led breast oncology as medical director at Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles before moving to UT Southwestern in 2021. She has mentored trainees and junior faculty on studies, two of which fed directly into NCCN treatment guidelines.

mccann.bio:
Dr. Kelly McCann is an associate professor and breast medical oncologist in the Division of Medical Oncology at UC San Diego, where she sees patients through UC San Diego Health. Her clinical interests center on breast cancer, including cancer genetics and risk assessment, and she has also listed gynecologic cancers and palliative care among her areas of interest. She holds board certifications in three areas: hematology, medical oncology and internal medicine.

Dr. McCann came to oncology through laboratory science, and her work bridges the bench and the clinic. Her doctoral research examined how cells repair double-strand breaks in DNA through homologous recombination, and as a fellow she investigated how PARP inhibitors work. She later coauthored preclinical and clinical findings on talazoparib combined with low-dose chemotherapy, along with reviews of targeted treatment for triple-negative breast cancer. More recently she has led real-world analyses comparing monthly and three-month goserelin dosing for premenopausal breast cancer patients, and a paper on which biomarkers best confirm that ovarian function suppression is working in ER-positive disease. She has also contributed to a multicenter study of immune-related side effects that appear late after immunotherapy for breast cancer.

She is active in professional education. Dr. McCann has recorded teaching series on sequencing therapy across HR-positive, HER2-positive and triple-negative breast cancer, took part in a 2026 case-based program on managing early HER2-positive disease, and helped write the report from the inaugural Bridging the Gaps in Breast Cancer Symposium, published in 2025. She has also spoken publicly about mentorship for women building careers in oncology.

Dr. McCann studied biomedical engineering at Rice University and then entered Stanford's Medical Scientist Training Program, earning an MD along with a doctorate in cancer biology. Her internal medicine residency was at OHSU in Portland, and she completed her hematology and oncology fellowship at UCLA. She remained at UCLA as an assistant clinical professor, working within the translational oncology research laboratories led by Dr. Dennis Slamon, before joining UC San Diego.

modi.bio:
Dr. Shanu Modi is a breast medical oncologist practicing at New York's Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK), where she has headed the Breast Medicine Service's section on HER2-positive disease. She also holds a faculty appointment as professor of medicine at Weill Cornell. Her clinical practice is devoted entirely to breast cancer, and she runs early-phase trials of new HER2-directed drugs.

Much of Dr. Modi's career has gone into developing new treatments that target HER2. She led DESTINY-Breast01, the pivotal study of trastuzumab deruxtecan for HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer that had already been treated, which supported the drug's accelerated FDA approval in 2019. She then led DESTINY-Breast04, the phase 3 trial that compared the same drug with standard chemotherapy in metastatic breast cancer with low levels of HER2. When she presented the results at ASCO in 2022, showing longer disease control and longer overall survival, the audience rose in a standing ovation, and the findings supported FDA approval for this newly defined HER2-low group of patients. At MSK she led DESTINY-Breast11, which tested the drug before surgery in stage II and III HER2-positive disease; together with DESTINY-Breast05 in patients with residual cancer after preoperative treatment, it underpinned the drug's May 2026 approval for HER2-positive breast cancer found at an early stage. She was also first author of a 2026 phase 2 study combining tucatinib with trastuzumab deruxtecan. Her earlier studies included early trials of HSP90 inhibitors such as ganetespib, laboratory work on the epichaperome, and trials pairing taxanes with trastuzumab and pertuzumab.

Dr. Modi helped write ASCO's 2014 clinical practice guidelines on systemic therapy for advanced HER2-positive breast cancer and on managing HER2-positive disease that has spread to the brain, as well as their 2018 updates. Her honors include a 2009 Advanced Clinical Research Award from ASCO's Conquer Cancer Foundation for her HSP90 research, and from 2009 to 2012 she held the Patricia and James Cayne Chair for Junior Faculty at MSK.

Dr. Modi earned her medical degree in Canada at the University of Alberta, where she also completed internal medicine residency, followed by medical oncology training at the Cross Cancer Institute. She then spent four years as a breast cancer research fellow at MSK and joined its Breast Medicine Service as full-time faculty in 2005. She also speaks to patient audiences about why trial participation and philanthropic support matter for progress in breast cancer.

moscol.bio:
Dr. Giancarlo Moscol is on the faculty of MD Anderson Cancer Center as an associate professor, holding a joint appointment in Breast Medical Oncology and in General Oncology. He sees patients at MD Anderson's location in The Woodlands, north of Houston, where his practice focuses on breast cancer alongside general medical oncology. He also holds an adjunct clinical faculty appointment in hematology and oncology at the University of Texas Medical Branch in Galveston.

Dr. Moscol takes part in MD Anderson's clinical research in breast cancer, with much of his recent work in early-stage triple-negative disease. He is a coauthor on studies that looked for blood-based immune markers of response to neoadjuvant pembrolizumab and chemotherapy, that used early changes in tumor volume to predict how patients will respond to the KEYNOTE-522 regimen, and that tested neoadjuvant sacituzumab govitecan with pembrolizumab (the NeoSACI-IO study) for patients whose tumors respond poorly to that standard approach. He has also contributed to work testing whether the CTS5 score can forecast late distant recurrence in hormone receptor-positive invasive lobular carcinoma, and he has cowritten book chapters on breast cancer, including one for a Cambridge text on gynecologic care of women with cancer.

Since 2018 Dr. Moscol has led the breast medical oncology tumor board at The Woodlands, and he takes part in MD Anderson's broader multidisciplinary breast tumor boards. He is the breast medical oncology liaison and a leader for MD Anderson's Project ECHO program, and he serves on the institution's IRB and on its HALs research steering committee. He reviews manuscripts for journals including Breast Cancer Research and Treatment, BMC Cancer and JCO Global Oncology. He lectures often on HER2-positive metastatic disease, triple-negative breast cancer and antibody-drug conjugates, including grand rounds in Houston, Ohio and the Cayman Islands, and has taught in Peru and Mexico as well as in community settings on screening and survivorship.

Dr. Moscol received his MD in 2006 from the National University of San Marcos (Lima) and practiced in Peru before coming to the United States. He completed internal medicine residency in Philadelphia and then spent two years as a clinical instructor on the bone marrow transplant unit at Thomas Jefferson University Hospital. He trained in hematology and medical oncology at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, where he received the Texas Society of Clinical Oncology's best fellow research award in 2015.

mouabbi.bio:
Dr. Jason Mouabbi is a breast medical oncologist and assistant professor at Houston's MD Anderson Cancer Center, appointed in both Breast Medical Oncology and General Oncology. His clinical practice concentrates on two groups of patients: people with invasive lobular carcinoma and people whose hormone receptor-positive breast cancer has spread.

Lobular breast cancer has been the thread running through Dr. Mouabbi's research since his residency. His work sets out to show how invasive lobular carcinoma differs from the more common ductal form, and to probe the biology of the cells and tissue surrounding these tumors, from the genetic to the molecular level, in search of treatments worth testing in trials. Recent projects he has led or contributed to at MD Anderson include a first-author study of how lobular tumors respond to neoadjuvant systemic therapy, a comparison of survival in metastatic lobular versus ductal disease (JAMA Network Open, 2025), an analysis of inherited mutations among 877 patients with lobular cancer, and a subgroup analysis of lobular tumors in the MONALEESA-3 trial of ribociclib with fulvestrant. Beyond lobular disease, he has worked on lung inflammation and loss of HER2 expression after trastuzumab deruxtecan, on HER2-low disease, on minimal residual disease testing, and on a trial that examined skipping breast surgery in exceptional responders to systemic therapy.

At MD Anderson, Dr. Mouabbi co-leads the working group on hormone receptor-positive breast cancer within Breast Medical Oncology and serves on MD Anderson's steering committee for advanced breast cancer. Nationally, he has led the Lobular Breast Cancer Alliance's Scientific Advisory Board as chair since 2023, participates in the Translational Breast Cancer Research Consortium's working group on ER-positive disease, and serves as an editorial board member for Oncology Data Advisor. He lectures widely on lobular and hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, including grand rounds in Texas, Louisiana and Canada. His recognitions include a Merit Award from the Lobular Breast Cancer Alliance (2025), a Breast Cancer Research Foundation scholarship, and a series of GRASP awards for linking researchers with patient advocates.

Dr. Mouabbi earned bachelor's and master's degrees in the biological sciences at Wayne State University in Detroit and his MD from St. George's University in Grenada. He completed internal medicine residency and a hematology and oncology fellowship at Ascension St. John Hospital in Detroit, serving as chief fellow, and then spent a year as a breast cancer clinical instructor at Baylor College of Medicine before joining MD Anderson.

odea.bio:
Dr. Anne O'Dea is a breast medical oncologist at KU Medical Center and the KU Cancer Center in Kansas City, where she serves as medical director of the breast cancer survivorship program. Her practice combines treatment of breast cancer with risk assessment, prevention and long-term survivorship care, and her patients come from both cities and rural communities across Kansas and neighboring states. She sees patients at KU clinics in Westwood and Overland Park, and she belongs to the cancer center's prevention and control research program.

Dr. O'Dea's research spans treatment trials and the needs of people after treatment. She has been involved in studies at KU that include SWOG S1501, which tested carvedilol for protecting the heart during HER2-targeted therapy for metastatic disease, the EMERALD trial of elacestrant, the MAINTAIN trial of ribociclib after progression on a CDK4/6 inhibitor, and the CompassHER2 RD trial of T-DM1 with or without tucatinib for residual disease. She is a coauthor of the NeoSTOP trial, which compared neoadjuvant carboplatin regimens with and without anthracyclines in triple-negative breast cancer, of an early-phase study of alpelisib with nab-paclitaxel, and of a single-cell genomics study of how resistance emerges during endocrine therapy combined with CDK4/6 inhibition. More recent coauthored work includes a phase 3 placebo-controlled trial that added a year of everolimus to endocrine therapy for high-risk early disease, the NeoPACT trial of preoperative pembrolizumab with carboplatin and docetaxel in triple-negative disease, and a randomized comparison of fixed-dose and standard-dose capecitabine; in 2026 she was senior author of a real-world analysis of stepping up the abemaciclib dose for patients with high-risk early disease. In survivorship, she has worked on KanSurvive, a model for delivering survivorship care in rural practices, on point-of-care genetic testing, on monitoring for lymphedema before it becomes established, and on measuring cognitive effort in survivors by tracking pupil responses.

Dr. O'Dea serves on SWOG's committee for breast cancer survivorship, prevention and epidemiology and on the breast disease working group at the KU Cancer Center. She previously served on the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education's committee on fellowship milestones and on a Commission on Cancer committee of the American College of Surgeons. She speaks regularly to both clinicians and patients: she gave the keynote at CURE's Educated Patient Breast Cancer Summit in 2023 on targeting ESR1 mutations, took part in a 2025 OncLive expert panel on HER2-positive breast cancer and brain metastases, and has spoken at community breast cancer awareness events in Kansas.

Dr. O'Dea trained entirely within the University of Kansas system, beginning with an undergraduate degree in human biology and continuing through her MD. She stayed at KU for internal medicine residency and for fellowship training in hematology and oncology, which included dedicated training in breast oncology. She is board certified in internal medicine, hematology and medical oncology.

oshaughnessy.bio:
Dr. Joyce O'Shaughnessy is a breast medical oncologist with Texas Oncology in Dallas, with her practice based at Baylor Charles A. Sammons Cancer Center. Both at Baylor Sammons and across The US Oncology Network, she leads breast cancer research as co-chair and heads breast cancer prevention research as chair, and she serves on US Oncology Research's scientific advisory board. She formerly chaired SCRI's breast cancer research executive committee (SCRI is the Sarah Cannon Research Institute) and now holds the title of chair emeritus. She also holds Baylor University Medical Center's Celebrating Women Chair in Breast Cancer Research. Her clinical work covers both the treatment and the prevention of breast cancer, and she divides her time between seeing patients and running clinical trials.

Over a career of four decades, Dr. O'Shaughnessy has taken part in the development of many drugs now used routinely in breast cancer. She was closely involved in the trials that brought capecitabine and gemcitabine into practice, and she has contributed to research on eribulin, the CDK4/6 inhibitors abemaciclib and ribociclib, pembrolizumab, and a range of HER2-directed and PARP-targeted agents. She also helped design risk-reduction studies that used tissue markers in women at high risk. Within The US Oncology Network she leads investigator-initiated phase 2 and 3 trials and helps shape industry-sponsored studies, while at Baylor she has run small translational trials in metastatic triple-negative disease that try to deepen defects in DNA repair so that tumors become more sensitive to chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

Education and drug-development policy have been constant threads in her work. She created, and has long directed, the School of Breast Oncology, an annual multi-day course devoted to the practical management of breast cancer, and she has chaired the program of the International Congress on the Future of Breast Cancer. Early in her career she coordinated a joint NCI and FDA working group on endpoints for approving cancer drugs, and she later chaired an AACR task force on treating intraepithelial neoplasia. She has served on ASCO's Board of Directors and as an associate editor of Clinical Breast Cancer. Her honors include the 2016 Giants of Cancer Care award for community outreach and education.

Dr. O'Shaughnessy did undergraduate work at the College of the Holy Cross, where she began laboratory research on leukemia, and earned her MD at Yale. Her internal medicine training was at Massachusetts General Hospital, followed by medical oncology fellowship training at NCI, the National Cancer Institute. She remained at NCI until 1995, including five years as a senior investigator leading breast cancer trials, and after a short period in practice in Louisville, Kentucky, she joined Texas Oncology in 1997.

pegram.bio:
Dr. Mark Pegram is a breast medical oncologist and translational investigator who now holds emeritus status on the medical oncology faculty of Stanford's School of Medicine, where his endowed title was the Suzy Yuan-Huey Hung Professorship in medical oncology. His clinical focus has been breast cancer and molecularly targeted therapy, and his clinical office is at Stanford's Women's Cancer Center.

Dr. Pegram's research has centered on HER2 and on new drugs for HER2-positive breast cancer, together with the question of why tumors become resistant to targeted treatment. He played a substantial part in bringing trastuzumab from the laboratory into the clinic: he led the preclinical studies showing that trastuzumab works synergistically with several chemotherapy drugs, and he was first author of the first phase 2 study pairing the antibody with chemotherapy. He was also a coauthor of the pivotal New England Journal of Medicine trials of trastuzumab with chemotherapy and of trastuzumab emtansine, and he was senior author on the registration trial combining lapatinib with letrozole, which led to FDA approval. More recently he was a coauthor of the HER2CLIMB trial of tucatinib, and at Stanford he has taken part in first-in-human studies of new HER2-directed agents. He has also devoted considerable effort to teaching clinicians about biosimilars and what they mean for cancer care.

At Stanford, Dr. Pegram served from 2013 as the cancer institute's associate director for clinical research, and he was appointed a School of Medicine associate dean responsible for the quality of clinical research in 2018 and medical director of the Clinical and Translational Research Unit, which runs first-in-human phase 1 trials, in 2020. Earlier he directed the Stanford Breast Oncology Program from 2012 to 2019 and co-directed the Translational Oncology Research Program. Nationally, he chaired the 2012 integration panel of the Breast Cancer Research Program run by the Department of Defense, and in 2025 he joined the breast cancer scientific committee of TRIO. His honors include the University of Miami's Sylvester Outstanding Cancer Research Award, the Connie Moskow Memorial Lectureship at Northwestern, the Hematology/Oncology Pharmacy Association's John G. Kuhn Lecture, a keynote at the American Radium Society's annual meeting, and a Breast Cancer Research Foundation award.

Dr. Pegram earned his medical degree at UNC Chapel Hill in 1986. He completed his internship and internal medicine residency at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas and his fellowship in hematology and oncology at UCLA in 1993.
