rao.bio:
Dr. Ruta Rao is a breast medical oncologist in Chicago and a professor of medicine at Rush Medical College, where her division is Hematology, Oncology and Cell Therapy. She serves as medical director of Rush University Cancer Center and directs the Coleman Foundation Comprehensive Breast Cancer Clinic at Rush. Her patients are seen at Rush University Medical Center and at Rush sites in Oak Park and Lisle, which have operated as RUSH MD Anderson Cancer Center since Rush and MD Anderson formed their partnership in 2024. She stresses care that treats the whole patient, bringing together medical and radiation oncology, surgery and psychosocial support.

Clinical trials are a large part of her work at Rush. Dr. Rao is the Rush site principal investigator for several national cooperative-group phase 3 studies now enrolling: ShortStop-HER2, an Alliance trial asking whether six months of HER2-targeted therapy can replace twelve for patients who have a pathologic complete response to preoperative treatment; an NRG Oncology trial testing whether adjuvant chemotherapy adds benefit to ovarian function suppression and endocrine therapy for premenopausal women with ER-positive, HER2-negative disease and a low Oncotype score; and an NRG Oncology study of online mindfulness programs for survivors. She is also the Rush contact for NSABP B-64, which studies blood tests for molecular residual disease, and she led an earlier Rush phase 2 trial of erlotinib in metastatic triple-negative breast cancer.

Her publications span treatment and outcomes research. She was first author of the ECOG-coordinated phase 3 intergroup trial that compared adjuvant tamoxifen with tamoxifen plus fenretinide in postmenopausal women, senior author of an early report on combining palbociclib with radiation for metastatic disease, and a coauthor of work on racial and ethnic disparities in delays to breast cancer treatment and on smoking cessation after breast reconstruction. In 2026 she was one of the expert panel authors of ASCO's updated guideline on surveillance and follow-up care once primary breast cancer treatment ends. She is a regular faculty member and commentator in clinical education, with recent programs on DESTINY-Breast11 and preoperative trastuzumab deruxtecan, on managing HER2-positive metastatic disease (including lung toxicity and screening for brain metastases), on the ASCENT trial and side effects of sacituzumab govitecan, and on circulating tumor DNA after surgery for early triple-negative breast cancer.

Dr. Rao completed medical school at the University of Wisconsin. She began postgraduate training in Los Angeles at USC and Los Angeles County, finished her internal medicine residency in Chicago at the University of Illinois, and then trained in hematology and medical oncology at Rush, where she has since risen through the faculty ranks from associate professor to professor.

rimawi.bio:
Dr. Mothaffar Rimawi is a medical oncologist who specializes in breast cancer and a professor of medicine in Houston at Baylor College of Medicine, where he belongs to the hematology and oncology section. He is Executive Medical Director of Baylor's Dan L Duncan Comprehensive Cancer Center as well as its associate director for clinical affairs, co-leads the center's breast cancer program, and is chief of oncology services for the St. Luke's Health system. He holds the Philip A. Salem, M.D. Chair in Cancer Research at Baylor St. Luke's Medical Center and sees patients on that campus; his clinical interests include HER2-positive and locally advanced disease, preoperative (neoadjuvant) treatment, and targeted therapy.

Dr. Rimawi describes his research as translational in both directions: taking laboratory discoveries into clinical trials, then returning patient samples from those trials to the lab for further study. His trials are built around biological rationale and intensive collection of tumor tissue, and he has identified and developed biomarkers that predict response and resistance to treatment. He has designed and led national and international trials in HER2-positive and estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, and this work has supported three broader shifts in the field: blocking HER2 with two agents at once, targeting the estrogen receptor at the same time as HER2, and scaling back treatment where it is safe to do so. He was first author of two Translational Breast Cancer Research Consortium trials, TBCRC 006 and TBCRC 023, that gave lapatinib and trastuzumab before surgery without chemotherapy (adding endocrine therapy for ER-positive tumors), and of follow-up work linking low PTEN and PIK3CA mutations to resistance to that approach.

Dr. Rimawi holds national research leadership roles: since 2022 he has been a vice chair of NRG Oncology's breast cancer committee, and he co-chairs the Translational Breast Cancer Research Consortium's working group on HER2-positive disease. In 2024 he joined the Scientific Advisory Board of the Lobular Breast Cancer Alliance. He speaks frequently on HER2-positive breast cancer, with commentary on trials such as NSABP B-52, KATHERINE, FeDeriCa and HER2CLIMB-02 and on preventing lung toxicity from HER2-directed drugs, and he presents cases at Baylor's breast and molecular tumor boards.

Dr. Rimawi earned his MD in Jordan, at the University of Jordan. He then completed his entire postgraduate training at Baylor College of Medicine: internal medicine residency, a fellowship in hematology and medical oncology, and an additional fellowship in breast cancer.

robson.bio:
Dr. Mark Robson heads the Breast Medicine Service at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center as its chief and holds a Weill Cornell Medical College appointment as professor of medicine. He is both a breast medical oncologist and a clinical geneticist, and his work centers on people who carry an inherited risk of cancer. His oncology practice leans toward young women with breast cancer, particularly hereditary breast cancer, and he also runs a separate clinic that organizes screening for women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations. Earlier in his MSK career he directed the clinic of the Clinical Genetics Service.

Dr. Robson's research asks how genetic information can be put to better use for women with breast cancer or at high risk of it. He was lead author of OlympiAD, an international phase 3 trial that tested the PARP inhibitor olaparib against standard single-agent chemotherapy in HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer with a germline BRCA mutation; the results were presented in the plenary session of the 2017 ASCO Annual Meeting, with a simultaneous New England Journal of Medicine publication. With colleagues he has also examined how hereditary breast cancer fares with breast-conserving treatment and with adjuvant chemotherapy, and how well breast MRI and ovarian cancer screening serve women at inherited risk. At MSK he is an investigator on an early-phase study of the experimental agent ART6043 and a co-investigator on a phase 3 trial pairing saruparib with camizestrant for metastatic disease.

His current work, supported by the Breast Cancer Research Foundation since 2006, follows two lines. One uses polygenic risk scores, combined with the CanRisk model, to give BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers more individual estimates of their risk, and is being extended to women with CHEK2, ATM or PALB2 variants. The other is a blood test for circulating tumor DNA intended for early detection and for tracking response to treatment, now being adapted for use in early disease that is ER-positive and HER2-negative.

Dr. Robson co-chaired the 2024 ASCO and Society of Surgical Oncology guideline on germline testing for patients with breast cancer, which calls for offering BRCA1 and BRCA2 testing to every newly diagnosed patient aged 65 or younger and to selected older patients. He studied at Washington and Lee University, earned his MD at the University of Virginia, and completed residency and fellowship at Walter Reed Army Medical Center. He came to MSK in 1996.

rugo.bio:
Dr. Hope Rugo is a breast cancer specialist, trained in both medical oncology and hematology, who has led breast medical oncology at City of Hope since 2025, serving as division chief and as director of the Women's Cancers Program across City of Hope's national network of academic and affiliated sites. She holds a professorship at City of Hope in medical oncology and therapeutics research and helps set the institution's clinical and translational research agenda in breast cancer.

As principal investigator, Dr. Rugo has led many trials that add new targeted drugs to standard therapy in both early and advanced breast cancer, with a focus on immunotherapy, endocrine therapy and drug combinations that overcome resistance. She has belonged to the I-SPY group of neoadjuvant trials since it began, helped design I-SPY2, and chairs that trial's safety committee. Her supportive care research changed practice: her studies helped bring scalp cooling into use to limit hair loss during chemotherapy and established a steroid mouthwash that prevents mouth sores from targeted agents. With funding from the Breast Cancer Research Foundation, her team studies how aggressive breast cancers escape the immune system, including the role of the MYC oncogene and what circulating tumor DNA reveals about tumor burden and response in I-SPY2 patients.

She has held leadership roles across major research groups. Within the Translational Breast Cancer Research Consortium (TBCRC), Dr. Rugo co-chaired the triple-negative working group and led several multicenter trials, and as an Alliance breast committee member she designed and ran a cooperative group phase 3 study. She has served as editor in chief of ASCO's Educational Book and co-chairs a study group on emerging toxicities for MASCC (Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer). She has also helped write ASCO and NCCN guidance on breast cancer treatment. She is a Fellow of ASCO, and her honors include ESMO's Breast Cancer Award in 2024, induction into the Giants of Cancer Care in 2020, and a Master Clinician Award from UCSF. For more than twenty years at UCSF she moderated an evening forum where patients and their families could learn about breast cancer.

Dr. Rugo earned a chemistry degree at Tufts University and her MD at Penn in 1984. She completed internal medicine residency and a hematology and oncology fellowship at UCSF, along with postdoctoral immunology research at Stanford. She joined the UCSF faculty in 1990 and spent her first nine years working in blood cancers and bone marrow transplantation before turning to breast cancer, eventually becoming director of breast oncology and of clinical trials education for UCSF's cancer center, a post she held until moving to City of Hope.

tarantino.bio:
Dr. Paolo Tarantino is a physician-investigator in breast cancer based in Boston, where he holds the title of advanced research fellow with the Breast Oncology Program of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Harvard Medical School. The focus of his work is the point where HER2 biology meets the development of antibody-drug conjugates.

Dr. Tarantino's research follows the HER2 protein across the spectrum of breast cancer, from tumors that overexpress it to the large group with only low levels, and asks how antibody-drug conjugates such as trastuzumab deruxtecan work and which biomarkers can predict who will benefit. He was first author of a 2020 Journal of Clinical Oncology review that laid out the pathology and clinical picture of HER2-low disease, and first author of the ESMO expert consensus statements on how to define, diagnose and manage HER2-low breast cancer (Annals of Oncology, 2023). His other first-author work includes a JAMA Oncology study of what low ERBB2 expression means for prognosis in early-stage disease, a genomic comparison of HER2-low and HER2-zero tumors in Nature Communications, an analysis of how HER2-low status shifts between primary and metastatic tumors, and a review in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians on antibody-drug conjugates across tumor types. In 2026 he was first author of the five-year follow-up of the Dana-Farber DAPHNe trial, which gave patients with stage II or III HER2-positive disease a shortened preoperative regimen of paclitaxel, trastuzumab and pertuzumab and tracked circulating tumor DNA with a highly sensitive assay. He contributes to both clinical trials and laboratory studies aimed at improving outcomes for patients with breast cancer.

Dr. Tarantino has been ESMO Open's associate editor for breast cancer since 2025, after serving as the journal's social media editor, and he is a frequent voice in professional education, discussing how to sequence and combine antibody-drug conjugates, the role of minimal residual disease testing, and key results from ASCO and ESMO meetings. He also explains these treatments for patient audiences, including resources on HER2-low disease and brain metastases. In 2025 he received OncoDaily's Yvonne Award, given in its Voice of Oncology category, and McGill University in Montreal named him its Vivian Saykaly Visiting Professor.

Dr. Tarantino earned his medical degree at the University of Naples Federico II. His medical oncology residency was through the University of Milan, based at Milan's European Institute of Oncology, where he joined the phase 1 team in 2018, and in 2024 he completed a clinical research PhD, also from the University of Milan. He then came to Dana-Farber and Harvard Medical School for advanced research fellowship training in breast oncology.

traina.bio:
Dr. Tiffany Traina is a breast medical oncologist in New York who has practiced with Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center's Breast Medicine Service since 2006. At MSK she is the Department of Medicine's Vice Chair of Outpatient Operations; during the COVID-19 pandemic she helped lead the return of the center's outpatient clinics to full activity. She also heads MSK's clinical research program in triple-negative breast cancer, and at Weill Cornell Medicine she holds the rank of associate professor of medicine.

Dr. Traina's research aims to develop better treatments for breast cancer, with a long-standing focus on triple-negative disease and on the androgen receptor as a drug target. She was first author of a study of the antiandrogen enzalutamide in triple-negative tumors that express the androgen receptor (Journal of Clinical Oncology, 2018), and with Rita Nanda of the University of Chicago she now leads a multicenter randomized phase 2 trial that tests enzalutamide, alone or with the glucocorticoid receptor blocker mifepristone, against chemotherapy for metastatic triple-negative disease that carries the androgen receptor; the Breast Cancer Research Foundation has supported her work since 2019. Her publications also include an early-phase trial of enzalutamide given alone or with endocrine therapy for advanced breast cancer, and she has contributed to work on male breast cancer as a biologically distinct disease, on the OncoKB precision oncology knowledge base, on adjuvant chemotherapy regimens that include eribulin, and on PD-L1 expression in the immune cells of triple-negative tumors.

Dr. Traina is a member of the working group on triple-negative disease in the Translational Breast Cancer Research Consortium. She is a Fellow of ASCO, and her awards include Susan G. Komen's Hally Yaccino Steiner Award and a Hero Award given by the Triple Negative Breast Cancer Foundation. She speaks regularly in educational programs, including sessions on HER2-positive disease that has spread to the brain and on building careers in breast oncology.

Dr. Traina earned her MD at Weill Cornell Medical College in 1999 and completed internal medicine residency at NewYork-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell. She then moved to Memorial Sloan Kettering to be chief medical resident, stayed for fellowship in hematology and oncology, and served as chief fellow in medical oncology before joining the breast medicine faculty.

tweed.bio:
Dr. Carol Tweed is a hematologist and medical oncologist with Maryland Oncology Hematology, based in Annapolis with additional clinic hours in Easton. She is board certified in both hematology and medical oncology and cares for patients with many kinds of blood disorders and cancers, while breast cancer remains the center of her practice. In 2022 she completed City of Hope's intensive genomic cancer risk assessment course, which certified her to evaluate inherited cancer risk, and she remains part of City of Hope's clinical genomics practice community.

Dr. Tweed has long combined community practice with clinical research. At Anne Arundel Medical Center in Annapolis she led many national and international trials as principal investigator, including cooperative group studies from ECOG, SWOG and Alliance and trials sponsored by the National Cancer Institute and Johns Hopkins. At Maryland Oncology Hematology she is the site principal investigator for a phase 2 trial combining tucatinib with liposomal doxorubicin in HER2-positive metastatic disease and for a phase 3b study of ribociclib with endocrine therapy in early breast cancer. Her recent coauthored papers address when PARP inhibitors fit breast cancers with somatic BRCA mutations, how health plans approach advanced disease with ESR1 mutations, and an ultrasensitive circulating tumor DNA test for residual disease after treatment; earlier, she was second author of a study asking whether genomic profiling could spare some postmenopausal women with ER-positive tumors a sentinel lymph node biopsy.

She serves as an ad hoc member of the breast cancer research executive committee at the Sarah Cannon Research Institute. She co-founded the Maryland Breast Cancer Consortium and serves as one of its co-directors, and she has been vice chair of the Adult Treatment Editorial Board for the National Cancer Institute's PDQ cancer information summaries. She speaks regionally and nationally on breast cancer and cancer genomics.

Dr. Tweed graduated summa cum laude from Duke University with a biology degree concentrated in molecular biology and was elected to Phi Beta Kappa. At Washington University in St. Louis she earned her MD and was inducted into Alpha Omega Alpha, and she completed internal medicine residency and a hematology and oncology fellowship at Penn. From 2006 to 2012 she was an assistant professor at Penn's Abramson Cancer Center, specializing in breast oncology and teaching students, residents and fellows. She then moved to Annapolis to practice with the Anne Arundel Medical Center oncology and hematology group, where she served on breast cancer leadership committees and precepted for Johns Hopkins, and in October 2020 she joined her current practice.

vidal.bio:
Dr. Gregory Vidal is a breast medical oncologist in Memphis who directs clinical research for both Regional One Health and West Cancer Center, where he also leads the breast cancer program. On the academic side, he is an associate professor in the Division of Oncology at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center College of Medicine. He treats breast cancer with chemotherapy, targeted drugs and immunotherapy, and he sees patients at the Midtown campus alongside Regional One Health and at West Cancer Center's East Campus in Germantown. He holds board certification in internal medicine, medical oncology and hematology.

Dr. Vidal's research centers on drug development and clinical trials in breast cancer, with the goal of finding better ways to diagnose and treat the disease. He was a coauthor of the randomized phase 2 ELAINE 1 trial, which compared lasofoxifene with fulvestrant in metastatic disease carrying an ESR1 mutation, and of a phase 2 study pairing fulvestrant with enzalutamide. A second focus is health equity. As first author he has examined how sociodemographic factors shape first-line treatment and outcomes for women with metastatic HR-positive, HER2-negative disease, how race and ethnicity affect timely genomic sequencing in community lung cancer care, and how a network of research sites can bring more people from underrepresented groups into trials. He also helped test a remote-monitoring app meant to help patients stay on endocrine therapy, along with related work on racial differences in symptoms and adherence. He has spoken about why Black patients in large trials such as RxPONDER can fare worse even with standardized treatment, pointing to later diagnosis, insurance and transportation barriers, conditions like diabetes, and mistrust of the health care system, and he sat on the planning committee for 2025's Summit on Cancer Health Disparities, where he co-chaired the abstract committee.

From 2022 through 2023 Dr. Vidal chaired the breast cancer disease group of OneOncology, which helped build clinical pathways for its member practices. He is a coauthor of ASCO's 2024 guideline on choosing germline genetic testing panels, sits on the editorial board of Breast Cancers Today, and was one of the program chairs of the 2026 West Oncology Conference. He lectures on breast cancer in the United States and abroad, takes part in expert education programs on topics such as sequencing therapy for HER2-positive metastatic disease and ovarian suppression for premenopausal patients, and in 2024 met with members of Congress about drug shortages and research funding. His early career recognition includes a KL2 career development award (2015), selection for the AACR and ASCO workshop on methods in clinical cancer research, membership in the Stanford Society of Physician Scholars, and a Department of Defense predoctoral training award.

Dr. Vidal earned bachelor's and master's degrees at the University of Mississippi and completed both an MD and a PhD at Tulane's medical school. At Stanford he trained in internal medicine and then in hematology and oncology, and he spent a year on the Stanford faculty before relocating to Memphis.

yan.bio:
Dr. Fengting Yan is a Seattle oncologist specializing in breast cancer at Fred Hutch Cancer Center, where she is a clinical associate professor in the Clinical Research Division, and she holds the same rank in the University of Washington's Division of Hematology and Oncology. She cares for patients with breast cancer at Fred Hutch's Sloan Clinic and at Fred Hutch at Overlake.

Dr. Yan leads several early-phase clinical studies as principal investigator, testing new treatment options in phase 1 and phase 2 trials for breast and ovarian cancer. She was first author of the phase 1 study that first gave patients PF-07260437, an experimental bispecific antibody that links T cells to the B7-H4 protein, in advanced breast, ovarian and endometrial cancers, and she was a coauthor of the Nature Medicine report on blocking the KAT6 enzyme in metastatic breast cancer that is ER-positive and HER2-negative, as well as a phase 2 trial testing zilovertamab vedotin across solid tumors. At Swedish she served as a site principal investigator for trials that included a phase 3 study of elacestrant in high-risk early breast cancer and Agendia's genomic data registry. Her recent writing covers practical management of side effects of the tucatinib, trastuzumab and capecitabine combination in metastatic HER2-positive disease, and the use of molecular residual disease testing to catch relapse earlier.

Her research interests are translational: finding molecular markers that drive women's cancers and developing drugs that block them. That approach grew out of years of laboratory work, including research at Ohio State that tested the enzyme PRMT5 as a drug target in lymphoma and earlier reproductive immunology research in Shanghai. Her commitment to women's health also reflects her first clinical specialty, obstetrics and gynecology, and a long record of public health education, including online outreach and appearances on television talk shows. She edits the breast oncology section of the International Journal of Cancer Care and Delivery, published by Binaytara, and sits on Binaytara's education committee; she also wrote the editorial for a Frontiers in Oncology collection of breast cancer case reports, and she has spoken on how genomic testing such as Oncotype DX guides treatment decisions.

Dr. Yan earned her medical degree in 1996 at Xi'an Medical University, where she also completed a master's degree in obstetrics and gynecology, and she received a PhD through the obstetrics and gynecology hospital of Fudan University. In the United States she completed internal medicine residency at The Ohio State University and a hematology and oncology fellowship through the University of Washington and Fred Hutch. She is board certified in internal medicine, hematology and medical oncology and is a Fellow of the American College of Physicians. Before joining Fred Hutch's faculty she practiced at the Swedish Cancer Institute's True Family Women's Cancer Center in Seattle.
